parts: Income is whatever comes into the family in the form of money – salary, part-time earnings, rent from a house or shop, bank interest, profit from shares and investments, earnings from skills or household produce. Using skills (stitching, kitchen garden, knitting) saves money that would have been paid out and adds to income; free facilities (medical, free education, rent-free accommodation) also save money. Family income is the income from all sources like salary of family members, rents, bank interest and savings from the use of family members' skills. Expenditure is the money spent from the income to meet needs – food, housing, clothing, education, transport, medical expenses, entertainment and others. Saving is the money set aside by the family for use in times of need (emergencies, children's education or marriage, old age, health).
Managing income and the spending plan

If expenditure is more than income the family has to borrow; if expenditure is less than income the family saves. Managing income means planning expenditure so that all needs are met within the income; the tool is a spending plan or budget – a list of requirements of family members with the money allocated to each, based on the total income. Steps: (1) keep in mind all income and facilities available for the period; (2) list all requirements; (3) prioritise the needs; (4) allocate funds keeping the total income in mind; (5) balance the plan; then keep records of all expenditure. Records help to know how much was spent on each item, control unnecessary expenditure, plan for the future, save money, compare prices and avoid being cheated.

Allocation depends on: income of the family; size of family (more members – more on food and clothing, less on entertainment); age of members (school-going children – education); place of residence (cost of living is higher in big cities); skills of members (fewer repair bills); and savings for the future. A guide table for an income of Rs 10,000 is: food 35% (Rs 3,500), housing 20% (Rs 2,000), clothing 5% (Rs 500), recreation 5% (Rs 500), household operations 6% (Rs 600), education 5% (Rs 500), transport 8% (Rs 800), medical 3% (Rs 300), furnishing 3% (Rs 300), savings 10% (Rs 1,000). It is advisable to save about 10% of the monthly income.

Balancing is making expenditure less than income, in two ways: earn more (tuitions, stitching, handicrafts, part-time job or overtime, kitchen garden, poultry, bee-keeping, making preserved foods) or cut expenditure (no food waste, less eating out, watch electricity and water use, iron and wash at home, economical use of stationery, public transport or cycle, public library, look for sales and rebates, shop in one trip, avoid impulsive buying, fund unnecessary items last). A spending plan discourages impulsive buying and helps meet all needs.

Accurate estimate of income (gross income differs from take-home pay); accurate estimate of expenditure (use past records); reasonably accurate allocation of money (anticipate festivals, etc.); and flexibility (a margin so that money can be diverted, for example from entertainment to an unexpected medical expense). A budget helps in living within income, achieving long-term goals, setting priorities and saving.
